text: Welcome back to the next part of the data engineering zoom camp.
Now so far what we've covered is building our first data engineering pipeline using Postgres.
And we've also been able to add a schedule to this and run backfields to fetch data from past
schedules. Now this data pipeline has been using ETL, also known as extract, transform and load.
This is where we extract the data from our source, in this case a CSV file stored on the web.
Then we transform it in our scenario we've been adding unique IDs and the file name to our data
before we then merge it into our final destination where we combine all the data together in the
load step. Now this is standard across the industry where pipelines that run on a nightly schedule
will run in this sort of format because it works very very well. However sometimes there are cases
where it may make sense to do things in a different order. Let's have a look at ELT. Now ELT
stands for extract, load, transform. So instead of transforming your data before you load it into
your final destination you actually load it into the destination first and then transform on top of
that data. Now the benefit here is this enables you to access things like the cloud where you can load
your massive data set into the cloud and then you can start transforming it with the power of
the cloud to help you. Now if any of you tried running the yellow data set using your PostgreSQL
setup you probably found it was incredibly slow because trying to add unique IDs to millions of rows
can take a beating especially on a personal laptop. So this is where we're going to start having a
look at how we can use BigQuery in the next few episodes to allow us to interact with that yellow
data set without it being such a hassle. So let's break it down. What does ELT really look like in
this scenario? So we're going to start off by extracting our data just like we did from GitHub.
We're going to make a HTTP request to get that CSV file. Now what we're going to do is load it into
a Google Cloud storage bucket which in this case we're going to use as a data lake. Now a data lake is
where we can store our data it doesn't need to be organized or sorted like it would in a database.
So in this case we can just put the CSV file straight in our data lake and we can come back to it
now if you'd love to learn more about data lakes we recently just did a video on it so I'd
recommend checking that out here now that we have our data in the cloud in our data lake what we can
do is now use our data warehouse which in this case is BigQuery to be able to map to that data lake
use that CSV file in it and now it can add some metadata on top this means the data stored in
the data lake but BigQuery is able to then utilize that data to perform our transformations and queries
as we wish. The reason this is faster is not only because we're utilizing the cloud which obviously
is typically faster than a computer that you might have at home but it isn't loading all of the data
into BigQuery instead it's just referencing it from the data lake which one helps to keep costs a
little bit lower but too it allows you to be able to perform big transformations without it getting
super slow. This means the original data stays untouched and you're just doing queries on top of
it so you get the benefit of cheap storage in this case the data lake rather than a database but
you get the power of the cloud to be able to get some insight into your data. Now in the next episode
we're going to look at how we can modify our workflow that we already have to now use ELT and
include Google Cloud Storage as our data lake and BigQuery as our data warehouse.
